question: How do a network's architecture and the training data jointly constrain the input-space geometry it can learn and thereby its simplicity and generalization biases?

key_findings.claim: The paper represents learned input geometry with an average gradient outer product and studies its parameter-gradient evolution rather than only the final predictor.
key_findings.evidence: It defines G_F as the parameter-and-data expectation of input-gradient outer products and Delta as its training-time change, linking eigendirections to decision-boundary sensitivity and input curvature.

key_findings.claim: At initialization, solvable wide networks align geometric evolution with data covariance filtered by architecture geometry.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 3.1 gives Delta approximately proportional to the sample covariance S for a one-hidden-layer ReLU MLP with an O(1/sqrt(Dn)) deviation; Theorem 3.2 gives the convolutional analogue GSG with O(1/n) deviation.

key_findings.claim: The proposed Geometric Inductive Bias hypothesis is broader than the proved initialization results and remains conjectural.
key_findings.evidence: Conjecture 1 generalizes the initial update to GSG, while Conjecture 2 says learned eigendirections remain within those supported by initial architecture geometry and data covariance; later experiments support but do not prove this invariant over training.

key_findings.claim: Synthetic feature-placement experiments show that what looks like simplicity bias depends on architecture-relative geometric accessibility.
key_findings.evidence: Across MLP, LeNet, ResNet-18, and ViT variants, generalization improves when a discriminative direction lies in a larger-eigenvalue direction of GSG; a nonlinear feature can be selected over a linear one when the latter is geometrically weak.

method.core_idea: Measure how training changes a model's input-gradient geometry and factor the accessible directions into an architecture term and the data covariance.
method.mechanism: Derive initial geometry evolution for wide one-layer MLPs and linear CNNs, conjecture a GSG factorization for general architectures, estimate its eigensystem numerically, and manipulate where class-relevant directions fall within that spectrum.
assumptions: Input-gradient outer products are a useful proxy for the geometry governing decision boundaries and generalization.
Initialization and early gradient-flow results predict directions available later in finite trained networks.
Squared-error scalar-output analysis transfers to classification losses and multiclass architectures.
Removing normalization layers does not erase the architecture effects under study.

techniques.role: Summarizes sensitive input directions through expected gradient outer products.
Differentiates that geometry with respect to parameters to characterize training-induced change.
Separates architecture geometry G from empirical data covariance S.
Places synthetic discriminants in strong or weak geometric directions to test generalization causally.

evaluations.setting: Wide one-hidden-layer ReLU MLP and linear CNN at initialization
evaluations.metric: Operator/Frobenius deviation of geometry evolution from S or GSG
evaluations.result: Theorems give concentration rates O(1/sqrt(Dn)) for the MLP and O(1/n) for the CNN

evaluations.setting: CIFAR-2 variants with MLP, LeNet, ResNet-18, and ViT without normalization
evaluations.metric: Alignment between measured Delta eigenspaces and GSG
evaluations.result: Reported correlations and eigenspace overlap support the initialization factorization across architectures

evaluations.metric: Test accuracy as the signal direction moves through the GSG spectrum
evaluations.result: Higher-eigenvalue directions generalize better and can reverse linear-versus-nonlinear feature preference
evaluations.baseline: Equal feature complexity without architecture-relative placement

evaluations.result: The proposed score yields a modest advantage, generally no more than about two percentage points in displayed experiments

limitations: The two central general-architecture statements are labeled conjectures rather than theorems.
Proofs cover one-hidden-layer scalar-output networks, initialization, squared-error loss, and gradient flow.
Normalization is removed from ResNet and ViT experiments even though it is standard and changes input geometry.
Most causal evidence uses binary synthetic relabelings of image data rather than naturally occurring features.
The sample-selection benefit is small and does not establish a practical data-curation advantage.
failure_modes: Normalization, attention softmax, or adaptive optimization may rotate geometry outside the initial GSG support.
Finite-width feature learning can create directions not predicted by an initialization statistic.
Average gradient geometry can obscure rare, class-conditional, or locally important directions.
A high-eigenvalue direction may be easy to learn yet spuriously correlated and harmful out of distribution.
reusable_insights: Express inductive bias relative to architecture and data jointly rather than calling a feature simple in isolation.
Test a geometric theory by moving the same label signal across its predicted eigendirections.
Separate proved initialization behavior from conjectured full-training invariants in downstream claims.
open_questions: Does the eigenspace containment survive normalization, residual scaling, Adam, and multiclass cross-entropy?
Can geometry measured before training predict natural spurious-feature selection or distribution shift?
What local or class-conditional geometry improves on the global average without becoming intractable?

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Anisotropy Directions
competitive_landscape.difference: Neural Anisotropy Directions identify architecture-induced input directions at initialization; the reviewed paper adds data covariance, training-time geometry evolution, and a GSG hypothesis.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Tangent Kernel: Convergence and Generalization in Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: NTK predicts function evolution from parameter gradients in an infinite-width lazy regime; the reviewed work studies input-gradient geometry and explicitly targets architecture-conditioned feature accessibility.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Spectral Bias of Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Spectral bias describes preference for low-frequency functions; the reviewed hypothesis argues that learnability depends on alignment with the architecture-and-data geometry, which need not coincide with frequency simplicity.

competitive_landscape.title: Tuning Frequency Bias in Neural Network Training with Nonuniform Data
competitive_landscape.difference: Yu et al. use NTK analysis to show how nonuniform data density changes frequency bias and how a Sobolev loss can tune it; the reviewed paper proposes a broader architecture-data input-geometry factorization beyond frequency alone.

novelty_assessment: The strongest novelty is the explicit GSG decomposition joining architecture anisotropy, data covariance, and input-geometry evolution, plus interventions that place the same signal in different predicted directions. The broad invariant is conjectural and the empirical scope omits standard normalization, so the work is a promising geometric research program rather than a settled general theory.
reviewer_notes: Read the definitions, proofs and theorem statements, GIB conjectures, synthetic and CIFAR-derived experiments, and limitations/appendices. Primary arXiv records for direct theory comparisons were checked on 2026-08-23.
